Hi! Thanks for reporting!
I've fixed this, now you can build according to same instruction.

Would also be great to get more information on how the server should be tuned - e.g. cache_coroutine, coroutine stack size.  Odyssey actually seems to be performing extremely well for us (thanks so much for open sourcing it!) -  but it'd be nice to have more information on this stuff.

E.g - Our logs look like this:
```
Sep 11 16:59:06   db-production-pooler odyssey[25946]: 25946 11 Sep 16:59:06.367 info [none   none] (stats) [] 1070 clients, 17 active servers,   128 idle servers, 9833 transactions/sec (1846 usec) 13236 queries/sec (416   usec) 3462817 in bytes/sec, 39753274 out bytes/sec

Sep 11 16:59:06 db-production-pooler   odyssey[25946]: 25946 11 Sep 16:59:06.367 info [none none] (stats) worker[1]:   msg (38317974 allocated, 0 cached, 38321752 freed, 0 cache_size), coroutines   (265 active, 22 cached), clients_processed: 3438
Sep 11 16:59:06 db-production-pooler   odyssey[25946]: 25946 11 Sep 16:59:06.367 info [none none] (stats) worker[2]:   msg (38672762 allocated, 0 cached, 38676373 freed, 0 cache_size), coroutines   (281 active, 25 cached), clients_processed: 3438
Sep 11 16:59:06 db-production-pooler   odyssey[25946]: 25946 11 Sep 16:59:06.367 info [none none] (stats) worker[0]:   msg (40125121 allocated, 0 cached, 40128711 freed, 0 cache_size), coroutines   (270 active, 17 cached), clients_processed: 3439
Sep 11 16:59:06 db-production-pooler   odyssey[25946]: 25946 11 Sep 16:59:06.366 info [none none] (stats) system   worker: msg (53175 allocated, 0 cached, 36689 freed, 0 cache_size),   coroutines (4 active, 1 cached)
```

Is that healthy? Why does it say 0 cached, 0 cache_size on the workers? (I don't think I disabled any caching - _actually, reading the code for this it seems it's hardcoded to 0?_)
This is on a 8-vcpu (4 core) machine with cache_coroutine 1200, coroutine_stack_size 4, 4 workers, 2 resolvers.

@MichaelRazum  - I'm not an expert on this, but I believe you'd want to configure workers to match your number of CPU cores available, similar to other event-driven servers like nginx. resolvers at 50 seems too high, I set it to 2 and it seems OK.   

Re pool_size , initially I set that to zero . It's not like connecting directly to the database if you use transaction pooling mode, as you'll still only create as many connections to the server as needed for how many of the client connections are actively executing a query or keeping a transaction open. However, I did see momentary spikes in connections happening (up to 800! - we have a very high max_connections on the postgres from not using a pooler before), so I'm trying with a pool_size limit of 300 instead.

We definitely need to update our docs and provide basic tutorials, sorry for that.

@MichaelRazum

`pool_size 0` would not set a limit on a number of connection in the pool, but will provide pooling functionality. In other words, connections will be reused as expected instead of making connection to a database each time. It might be useful to set connection limit on a PostgreSQL side as well, in that case Odyssey will forward any connection errors to clients.

`workers N` it is hard to tell for sure, how much workers you will need. It might makes sense to start from smaller value and just increase it if you see that there are high cpu usage or have a periodic connection spikes, etc. In production environment we set workers to something like `CPU cores / 2` to automate this process. @x4m might provide better information regarding the configuration.

You can choose your own method to start Odyssey or take a look at existing support to do it in script dir: https://github.com/yandex/odyssey/tree/master/scripts. We used to build dev and rpm packages. 

@jordan-thoms 

Thank you for your feedback! Yes, stats looks healthy :) basically they are for developers mostly and I would not worry to much about them, I guess we need to make an additional option to disable them. They could be useful to track memory usage per worker, since there we put a lot of effort to keep it low and avoid malloc/fragmentation issues in multi-threaded environment.

Basically increasing resolvers will create additional threads to execute `getaddrinfo()` to avoid blocking coroutine/process execution. It might be needed to increase this number if you have PostgreSQL server run not on the same host which runs Odyssey, which is a very rare situation I believe.

Thanks for that! Actually I did deploy odyssey on a separate server, I have it at the moment with a bunch of pods running on Kubernetes, pointing to a VM with Odyssey, which is then pointing to the DB on another VM. I guess my thinking there was that it would reduce the chance that high DB load could starve the pooler of CPU.  I'm not seeing any delays in resolve times in the logs though so that's all good.

Is there a stat for how long clients have been waiting for a server connection to be available? I set a pool_size of 300, and that's removed the connection spikes on postgres but now I have a few very short lived times (~10s or less) where there are 300 active server connections and none idle (usually it sits at ~20 active). I guess that is probably from a spike in clients keeping transactions open for a longer period.

Odyssey is partly compatible with PgBouncer console commands. For example following commands should work: `SHOW STATS, SHOW POOLS, SHOW SERVERS, SHOW CLIENTS, SHOW LISTS`. Probably `SHOW STATS` is what you are looking for, but some metrics could not be implemented yet.

Hi,

Odyssey is mostly compatible with PgBouncer administrative console, so most likely everything will work out of the box. If something is not working, I am sure that can be easily added or fixed. It is worth to try :)

Sounds good. The pgbouncer exporter code basically runs `SHOW` on several subsystems.

You can [see the column mapping here](https://github.com/stanhu/pgbouncer_exporter/blob/ef1fb717f6e7c910def61904738a7c534ae2f00b/collector.go#L19-L55)
There's no ```show databases``` for now, but it's quite easy to add it.

While it's nice to be compatible with pgbouncer, it might be worth the effort to provide a "real" Prometheus metrics endpoint. For example, there is a [C library](https://github.com/digitalocean/prometheus-client-c) that can be used.

This way monitor isn't in-line with database connections. It's also possible to expose a lot more interesting data than is possible with just the pgbouncer-compatible metrics. For example, Prometheus supports histograms, so relatively cheap heatmap data can be exposed from the odyssey instances.

It certainly makes sense to provide "plugin system" for monitoring connections and make some examples string with Prometheus.
But adding show databases is way easier...
